title: Vote intention
text:
This report covers vote intention: 500 respondents across 5 waves (1 to 5). Vote intention is a categorical outcome with 9 response categories plus a “Missing” category. The categories “Would not vote” and “Undecided” were only offered from wave 2, so wave 1 cannot be compared with later waves for those two categories.
Disclosure rules (decision D22, extended): counts of 1 to 9 are shown as “<10”. Because the number of respondents is stated, a table with one hidden cell in a row or column also hides the smallest visible positive cell there (“suppressed”), so no hidden cell can be recovered by subtraction. Zero counts are shown as 0.

title: Social dominance orientation
section: Can scores be compared across waves?
text:
Can scores be compared across waves?
For this construct, the same 8 items with the same wording appear in every wave, and the response scale is 1 to 7 in all of them (one range for all items). Documented non-answer codes: none. The repository’s validation checks (decision log D01 to D16) found no differences in wording, response options or range between waves. Wave scores are therefore on the same metric, and mean-level comparison across waves is defensible. This establishes that the scores are comparable on paper; it does not show measurement invariance, which would need a longitudinal factor model and is listed as a limitation.

text:
Mixed-model estimate of change
As a complement to the pairwise contrasts, a linear mixed model estimates the mean at each wave with a random intercept per respondent: score ~ wave (factor) + (1 | respondent), fitted by REML with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. All available observations are used, so no balanced panel is assumed. The table gives the wave 1 mean and the change from wave 1 at each later wave with 95% confidence intervals. The intraclass correlation (ICC) is the share of variance due to stable differences between respondents. The contrasts are unadjusted for multiple comparisons, so a few intervals excluding 0 are expected by chance. Estimates are associations in observed scores and do not address measurement invariance (see the comparability statement above).

title: How I would work at PPBS
text:
My interest in political behaviour grew out of a question I worked on during the pandemic: how does a large societal shock relate to everyday prosocial behaviour? In that study (Vieira, Pierzchajlo, et al., 2022, Scientific Reports), we collected four independent online samples, one week apart, in spring 2020. We analysed the data using mixed models and simulation-based power analysis in R. One limitation we noted was that using independent samples made it difficult to detect changes within individuals over time. A panel following the same participants would help address this limitation, which is one reason this exercise interests me.
My background is not specifically in political psychology, although political behaviour has been an area of interest throughout my PhD. I would bring experience in quantitative research, statistical modelling and reproducible research practices, as well as experience working with complex datasets.

Reproducibility. I founded a ReproducibiliTea journal club at Stockholm University, where I organised meetings and led discussions. I also regularly share code and data through GitHub and OSF. The data and code from the study mentioned above are publicly available.
Modelling. I mainly work in R and have experience with mixed models, simulation-based power analysis and Bayesian multilevel models. I have also taught statistics at bachelor’s, master’s and PhD level.
Complex data. I have combined data from different sources into analysis-ready datasets and worked with standardised data structures and preprocessing workflows, including BIDS and Docker for fMRI data. More recently, I have worked with large language model outputs, combining them with survey and psychophysics data.

System
What I would do




Qualtrics
I would keep the QSF files and exports under version control. title: How I would work at PPBS
text:
Two concrete improvements

1. An item specification to support automated checks and review
Current setup. The file config/item_spec.csv contains information about each item, including its construct, wording, valid range, non-answer codes and the waves in which it appears. It also records the keying described in the guide separately from the keying applied in the data. The existing checks read from this file, meaning that adding a construct or wave can be handled by updating the specification rather than changing the analysis code.
Example from this exercise. The guide lists items as inversely coded for four of the five constructs. When I applied these reversals, reliability was close to or below zero, with negative item-rest correlations. Without reversing the items, reliability was acceptable and all inter-item correlations were positive. This suggested that the extract had already been recoded. I therefore left the item values unchanged, retained the keying described in the guide in a separate column, and recorded the issue in the decision log (D17).
I identified this through the scale checks I ran for the exercise. I would extend these checks so they run automatically for every construct and wave. If an item behaves unexpectedly, it would be flagged for review, with the item, wave, expected behaviour and observed results recorded. This would give someone a clear starting point for investigating the issue without allowing the script to make potentially incorrect corrections automatically.
What I would do in the first week:

Preserve the original source files, existing codebook and decision log format.
Adapt the checks to read directly from the item specification and add a reviewer queue to the repository.
Compare the automated reliability calculations against my hand calculation for one construct and wave, and test whether the checks flag an intentionally misconfigured item.
Run the checks on the approved full dataset and have a research lead review and resolve the flagged items.



2. Making the build more efficient and easier to restart
Current setup. The current entry point is source(“run.R”). It processes the scores, runs the tests, renders the site and checks the output for potential data leaks. It stops if a step fails, but currently reruns the entire workflow each time.
What I would change. I would move the workflow to targets, which would track dependencies between steps and only rerun those affected by a change. For example, correcting one item would trigger the relevant scoring and analyses without requiring every report to be rebuilt. Scoring and model fitting could also be kept separate from report generation. For larger datasets, the pipeline could be configured to run across multiple workers on a computing cluster. I would retain renv to keep package versions consistent.
What I would do in the first week. Keep run.R as the entry point and retain the existing tests, while changing the underlying workflow to use targets. I would compare the resulting processed scores against those produced by the current script to check that they are identical on the exercise data. I would then document how to run the pipeline on the approved full dataset.
I have not built the targets version yet. This is a proposed improvement, not something I have already implemented.

title: How I would work at PPBS
text:
Tools I could use
I would continue using R as the main environment for the analysis. renv would manage package versions, targets would handle dependencies between analysis steps, and Quarto would be useful for generating reports. For scale evaluation and factor models, I would use packages such as psych and lavaan. testthat would support automated checks, while brms or Stan could be used for Bayesian multilevel models where appropriate.
For reporting model results, I would also consider marginaleffects and packages from the easystats collection, such as parameters, performance and effectsize. Regardless of the package, I would check important outputs against simpler calculations where possible, as I did with the reliability calculations in this exercise.

title: How I would work at PPBS
section: Decisions I would make myself, and decisions for a research lead
text:
Decisions I would make myself, and decisions for a research lead
There are several parts of the workflow I would be comfortable managing independently. These include file naming and organisation, writing and maintaining tests, documenting limitations, deciding how to present uncertainty, and following existing written procedures.
Other decisions have implications for the research itself and should involve a research lead:

Whether items that appear to have already been recoded should become the documented standard (D17).
How to handle columns that are not explained in the existing guide.
Whether attrition in the full dataset affects the choice between a balanced panel and an available-case analysis.
Changes to coding that could alter previously published PPBS results.
Decisions about disclosure thresholds and which results or data can appear on the public site.
